content:
We have discussed the issue of USB-C cables many times: they may look identical on the outside, but their actual capabilities can vary wildly.

Google solved this problem in Chrome OS years ago, and we suggested at the time that Apple should follow suit. Apple still hasn't done so, but there's now a free Mac app called WhatCable that can turn your Mac into a hardware cable tester…

These days, just about every electronic device we buy comes with a USB-C cable in the box, making it easy to accumulate a whole drawer full of them with no idea which to use when a specific function is needed. Each cable can have different limits for the following:

  • Data transfer speed
  • Video bandwidth
  • Power delivery

At one end of the spectrum, you can buy cables that support 40Gb/s data transfer speeds, 8K 60Hz video output, and 240W power delivery; at the other end are charge-only cables, and low-speed cables with a data transfer limit of just 480Mbps.

Hardware cable testers are available for purchase and can report the capabilities of a connected cable, but now there's a free Mac app that does the same thing. WhatCable works by measuring the actual performance of a cable while it's in use, or—as the "Mac charging itself" joke goes—by plugging the cable from one USB-C port on the Mac to another.

It can also read the identification data from the chip built into the cable to determine the manufacturer and whether it is USB-IF certified. Note that a lack of certification may mean the cable is counterfeit, but it may also simply mean the manufacturer has chosen not to pay for certification.

The app works because the Mac already reads these capability details from the built-in chip. WhatCable makes it easy to access this data and translates everything into plain language.

See whether your current charging speed is being limited by the cable, the charger, or the Mac, and see the negotiated power specs. Work out in plain language whether the Mac port, the cable, or the device is the bottleneck, so you know whether swapping in a faster cable would actually help. When connecting a display, see whether you're getting the full resolution and refresh rate, or something less, and whether the limitation is the adapter, the cable, or the mode you've selected. Decode cable speed, current rating, manufacturer identity, and USB PD capability markers from marked USB-C cables.

The free version does all of the above, while the Pro version offers more detailed information, such as real-time negotiation details for each connection, showing how and why two devices end up operating at a particular charging or transfer speed. The Pro version is a one-time purchase of £9.99 (around $13.40).

Sean Hollister of The Verge tested it and found it performs well, though not perfectly, as some cables misrepresent their capabilities.
